fields.question: What is "transpilation"?
options: Compiling JavaScript down to machine code for the CPU
Translating source code into other source code, such as TypeScript into JavaScript
Removing whitespace and shortening names to reduce file size
Combining many modules into a single output file
fields.hint: Ask what language the output is written in. Two of these options describe changes to size or file count instead.
fields.explanation: Transpilation is source-to-source compilation: TypeScript to JavaScript, JSX to function calls, or modern syntax down to what your browser targets support. Minification and bundling also run in a build, but they shrink and combine output rather than translate the language, and producing machine code is the engine's JIT at run time, not a build step. Which syntax gets downleveled is a configuration choice (tsconfig target, browserslist), not a fixed rule.

notes: Key text trimmed to one example so the longest-option cue disappears; index unchanged.

options: The JavaScript language specification that defines the syntax
The engine that executes the code plus the host's built-in APIs
Only the parser that turns source text into a syntax tree

fields.hint: The same file can run in one host and throw ReferenceError in the other. Ask what differs, given the language is identical.
fields.explanation: A runtime is the engine that executes your code together with the APIs its host exposes: window, document and fetch in a browser; process, fs and Buffer in Node. The language specification defines only the syntax and the built-ins both hosts share, and the parser is one stage inside the engine rather than the whole environment. This is why the same file can run in one host and throw ReferenceError in the other, and why 'works in Node' says nothing about the browser.

options: Only a runtime that executes any program without conventions
A web framework that supplies structure and common application plumbing
A utility library whose functions the project calls when it needs them
A build tool that compiles and bundles the project's assets
fields.hint: Match the breadth of what the toolkit supplies against what each kind of tool is normally responsible for.
fields.explanation: A web framework supplies reusable code plus conventions for the concerns every application repeats — routing, request handling, configuration, project layout — and it calls your code at the points it defines. A runtime executes whatever program you hand it and imposes none of that structure. A library waits to be called and shapes nothing on its own, and a build tool decides what the output files look like rather than how the application is organized.

problems: two options ('a database driver limited to sending queries', 'a browser engine that renders the server's source code') are category errors, so the item was answerable by elimination; the rewrite touched only hint and explanation and left them in place

evidence: knowledge: framework versus library is defined by which side owns control flow; a build tool shapes output artifacts, not application structure
notes: The library option is the real near miss for this stem, so the replacement also raises what the item teaches.

fields.explanation: The distinguishing property is inversion of control — you decide when to call a library function, while a framework owns the flow and calls your route handler, component or lifecycle hook at moments it defines. Size and where the code runs do not separate them: React runs in the browser and behaves like a framework, lodash runs anywhere and is a library. The reversed statement, that the library imposes the structure, is the usual mistake.

fields.explanation: Frontend code is delivered to the browser and runs there, on the user's machine — which is why anyone can read it, modify it, or replay the requests it makes, and why it can hold no secrets. Server-side rendering runs the same components on the server to produce the initial HTML, but the interactive code still runs in the browser afterwards. A CDN delivers those files to the browser rather than running them.

fields.explanation: The API contract is the agreement between the two programs: which endpoints exist, what they accept, what they return, and how errors are reported. The wire format and the client's HTTP library carry the request, but neither decides which endpoints exist or what they return.

fields.hint: An index makes the database bigger, not smaller. Start from there.

problems: hint states both halves of the key ('what the engine avoids doing once the index exists, and what it now has to maintain on every write')
evidence: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/indexes-intro.html — without an index 'the system would have to scan the entire test1 table, row by row'; 'After an index is created, the system has to keep it synchronized with the table. This adds overhead to data manipulation operations'; 'indexes that are seldom or never used in queries should be removed'
notes: The physical-order distractor is true of a clustered index in InnoDB or SQL Server, but the stem asks why you would add one and the explanation limits its claim to PostgreSQL; worth watching if the item is ever reused engine-neutrally.

fields.hint: Two of the four ACID properties are at work here. Start with what the A stands for.

problems: hint ('picture the transfer failing between the debit and the credit — what must the database promise?') leads straight to all-or-nothing without any knowledge
evidence: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/tutorial-transactions.html — 'The essential point of a transaction is that it bundles multiple steps into a single, all-or-nothing operation'; 'The intermediate states between the steps are not visible to other concurrent transactions'
knowledge: how much recent data a transaction sees depends on isolation level, which is why READ COMMITTED and SERIALIZABLE differ
